items.body:
Unity, spirit and diversity are three words that perfectly describe IShowSpeed’s vibrant contribution to the already epic FIFA World Cup 2026 soundtrack. His track 'World Cup (Champions)' creates the perfect banger with its mix of uplifting beats and swelling melodies, topped with his booming, enthusiastic voice delivering the empowering lyrics.

"One moment, one dream, cos it's that time, let's go!" he chants at the beginning of the track, capturing the incredible passion and fervour that people all over the world have for the World Cup season. The song represents the unanimous love for the sport as it unites people regardless of background, race and language, as they all bask in the glory of their respective flags.

The accompanying music video for the track was filmed in Miami Stadium during IShowSpeed's world tour, as he goes on to shout out countries like Ghana, Portugal, Brazil, Australia, Austria, Bosnia, Colombia, Argentina and so many more. The roaring lyrics capture the explosive energy of the World Cup season as they say, "Cos this is the World Cup, put your flags up in the air, put your hands up in the air, put your flags up, cos this is the World Cup..."

Within days of the song's release on 1 June, the video hit over 19 million YouTube views, even exceeding the view counts of official FIFA anthems on various social media platforms. Riding the wave of the song's remarkable success, IShowSpeed took to X to tag the official FIFA World Cup account, suggesting that the track be included on the Official FIFA World Cup 2026 Album. FIFA fuelled speculation when it replied with a simple, "We will be in touch."

can we make this official ?? @FIFAWorldCup https://t.co/qH7p5CawGi

— Speed⭐️ (@ishowspeedsui) June 1, 2026

Fans were quick to express their excitement at the possibility of seeing 'World Cup (Champions)' become part of the tournament's official soundtrack. One supporter praised the idea, writing, "Since FIFA said they'd be in touch about making this official, I just gotta say that I really couldn't think of anyone better to represent the World Cup than the guy who's spent the last three years promoting and learning the world's cultures and breaking stereotypes around them."

On 3 June, IShowSpeed opened a DM from the official FIFA World Cup Instagram account on a livestream, the message read, "We heard it. We liked it. It’s on the Official FIFA World Cup 2026 Album," as he cheered and celebrated the incredible milestone his track has achieved. The song takes its place among bangers such as 'Goals' by BLACKPINK's LISA, Anitta and Rema, 'Game Time' by Tyla and Future, 'Echo' by Daddy Yankee and Shenseea and more.

IShowSpeed received a DM from the FIFA World Cup account revealing they put his new World Cup song on the official Album 🔥

"We heard it. We liked it. It's on the Official FIFA World Cup 2026 Album" pic.twitter.com/XyessVzAcy

— yoxic (@yoxics) June 3, 2026

With 'World Cup (Champions)' securing its place on the Official FIFA World Cup 2026 Album, IShowSpeed has transformed his passion for the sport into a global anthem that resonates far beyond the pitch.

Summer just got a little brighter. YGIG have returned with their latest single, 'Perfect Blue' on Underdog Music, a dance-pop release that captures the carefree energy of the season while leaning into the group's evolving sound.

The track pairs upbeat rhythms with tropical-inspired production, creating a breezy soundtrack fit for sun-soaked days and late-night memories. While undeniably playful, 'Perfect Blue' also carries a sense of nostalgia, reflecting on fleeting moments and connections that linger long after summer ends.

Anchored by lyrics such as "Swimmin' through the waves of love" and "Let's keep dancin' until June," the song balances feel-good energy with emotional depth. The release also arrives alongside a new TikTok campaign, with YGIG encouraging fans to join in on a dance challenge inspired by the track's infectious chorus.

Composed of VIEN, HAZELYN, JEWEL, and MAEG, YGIG continue to carve out their place in the P-pop scene through a growing catalogue that includes fan favourites such as 'Shaba Shaba', 'Doob Doob', and 'Universe'. With 'Perfect Blue', the quartet embrace a brighter and more playful sonic direction while staying true to their signature cool-girl identity.

items.body: 6YPAH (spreek uit als Buran) haalt zijn naam bij het Russische ruimteprogamma al komt de band wel uit Slovenië. Opgericht in 2008 start het duo Jani Toplaki en Giorgio Multineddu (Italiaan van geboorte) het rommelen met analoge synths om later gitaar en andere instrumenten toe te voegen en tot een eigen post punk, new wave taal te komen. Van alle projecten bij Final Muzik moet deze 6YPAH zowat het meest toegankelijke zijn. Het zal tot in 2023 duren vooraleer er fysiek materiaal, “Electronic Visions Across The Border” verschijnt in eigen beheer en nu is er deze “Prozorno Mesta” (te vertalen als transparante stad), dat in 2025 verscheen maar nu dus wordt opgepikt door het Final Muzik label. Wat ik hoor zijn zes, eerder poppy verpakte post punk songs, die uitgerust met een elektronische ruggengraat, zowel genres als post punk, new wave tot dark wave aftasten. Dat resulteert in een moderne Kraftwerk (ehum) track als “Supersila” die bol staat van synth pop ivloeden tot een typische post punk / dark wave track als “Neugörz”, een jonge, moderne stad in het westen van Slovenië, direct gelegen aan de grens met de Italiaanse stad Gorizia, waar de wieg van 6YPAH staat. In “Supersila” krijgt wijlen Ronald Reagan een hoofdrol. Politiek en maatschappij, het zou een vak in elke school moeten zijn, is het duo alvast niet vreemd getuige ook de titel “Distopija” waarmee het eindresultaat van de utopie kapitalisme en de utopie communisme wordt samengevat op een ietwat gelaten, vereenzaamde synth lijn. “‘Ustanova” (rust) waarmee het album opent kent een lange aanloop die naar kraut rock lijkt te lonken om eens over de drie minuten ietwat wispelturig een post punk steegje in te duiken en te eindigen met een soort kanarie robots die een ‘endzeit’ riedel tsjierpen. De meest romantische nummers “Veno S Tabo” (te vertalen als ‘altijd bij je’) en Pod Nebom (te vertalen als ‘onder de hemel') kennen in de verte een Molchat Doma Echo. Wat dit album, of moet ik met (slechts) zes nummers eerder over een uit de kluiten gewassen ep spreken, aangenaam om luisteren maakt is dat elk nummer weer net anders klinkt waardoor “Prozorno Mesta” nooit gaat vervelen maar de volle 29 minuten interessant blijft in een eigenzinnige mix van synth pop, new wave en post punk. Naar Final Muzik normen dus een zeer toegankelijke release van een bij ons totaal onbekend duo 6YPAH. Liefhebbers van ‘zachte’ post punk moeten dit zeker eens proberen. Prozorno Mesto by 6YPAH 6YPAH

items.body:
Home/Reviews/Accident Fantôme
ACCIDENT FANTÔME — OBJETS ENCHÂSSÉS DANS DES ANNEAUX PLANÉTAIRES( OBJECTS EMBEDDED IN A PLANETARY RING )
[moli del tro — 2026]
★
★
★
★
★
Reviewed 5 June 2026
by Colin Lang
Artist website →

Accident Fantôme is the portmanteau for the project of two otherwise autonomous, established musical duos, Accident du Travail and Fantôme Josepha. United by shared interests in historical instruments and long-form, ambient drone composition, the four gathered in an old church in a village just west of Metz (where some of the group are based) early last year to perform and record together.

The ecclesiastical setting was selected for its mid-19th-century pipe organ — the instrument par excellence of the dronies — along with its remoteness, outside of the hustle and bustle, though situated near the Front of the First World War and all its spectres. In addition to said organ, Objects Embedded in a Planetary Ring features guitar, harp, and the ondes Martenot, one of the earliest electric instruments, which, following in its use by Messiaen, Boulez, and others, has become something of a cult object among French classicists.

“Cosmos“: the opening track, is a swirl of harp and organ, pulling heavenward with little to no anchor, so that when an electric guitar struts its way into the mix, we get a bit more electronics and processing along with it. The whole thing is drowning in reverb, whether added through effects or culled from the church environs, it makes for an engrossing if familiar haze. “Euphorie”, the longest of the five compositions, leans pretty heavily into the organ, a single chord depressed, vibrating and blanketing the empty space into which it moans. Here, we get the clearest picture of the theremin-like whirling of the ondes Martenot, which takes us out of the house of worship and onto Mars. All of this ushers in some higher frequency squeaks before Brother Pipes takes control of the party. The last piece, “Brief Whistling” is just that, something straight out of a Morricone Western, Cinecittà suddenly rolling over the graves of unnamed soldiers.

Fans of lowkey drone and the cinematic side of ambient work should find plenty to scratch that itch. Others interested in the otherworldly beauty of the ondes Martenot should probably tune in too.

items.body:
Home/Reviews/Luigi Nono/Roberto Fabbriciani
LUIGI NONO/ROBERTO FABBRICIANI — LUIGI NONO VOLUME 2: WORKS WITH FLUTE
[Mode Records — 2026]
★
★
★
★
★
Reviewed 5 June 2026
by Roger Batty

Here’s a CD serving up three works for flute composed by Italian avant-garde/ modern classical composer Luigi Nono (1924- 1990), with a fourth by Nono collaborator Roberto Fabbriciani, who also plays flute/ piccolo here. The sound on offer here is a nice mix of moodily seared, eerily abstract, and tautly ambient, with a great use of compositional space.

Here from Mode is a CD presented in a jewel case. It comes with a twelve-page inlay booklet- this takes in write-ups about the pieces/ composers, photos of Nono & Fabbriciani, and photos of some of the scores.

We open with 1985’s “A Pierre. Dell’azzurro silenzio, inquietum” which is for contrabass ﬂute in G, contrabass clarinet in B ﬂat, and live electronics. The just over eight-minute track is all about steadily baying and searing wind instruments, with an undercurrent of subtly warping & uneasy electronics. It brought to mind a more ambient take on the material Wolf Eyes did with Anthony Braxton.

Next is 1980/87’s “Das atmende Klarsein, fragmente”, this is for bass flute, magnetic tape, and live electronics. Here we find a very taut and tensioned soundscape of stretched warbles, pulled out hisses, strangled piping’s, and grating flits. It runs at just over the seventeen-minute mark- keep its tight reining in your attention throughout, even when space & silence are used briefly.

Track three is the oldest composition here, “Musiche per Manzù”. It runs at just over the seventeen-and-a-half-minute mark and is for magnetic tape. Here we find a stark blend of ringing slabs of tone, cascading rattle ‘n’ bay, with moments of reverberating rounding, jarring/ loud bass darts, and what sounds like forlorn vocalising. I’m guessing flutes were involved at some point in the tracks' creation, but it doesn't really retain much of the instruments' sonic identity. There is certainly a proto noise feel to this track, especially in the more loud/ overloaded moments

Finally, we have “A Omaggio a Luigi Nono”, which is composed by Roberto Fabbriciani. It dates from 2006. It’s for Piccolo, tape, and live electronics. This comes in at dead on the twelve-minute mark. The piece is built around the steadily warbling and baying sound field, which is both sour, sometimes shrill, but always uneasy. You keep thinking that something large or big-sounding is going to suddenly appear, or the sound picture is going dense up-, but it never does.

If you enjoy where shrill & sear meet uneasy psycho ambient, I think this four-track collection will appeal.

items.body:
Home/Reviews/David First
DAVID FIRST — REVOLUTIONS
[Mode Records — 2025]
★
★
★
★
★
Reviewed 5 June 2026
by Roger Batty

Revolutions is a long-form drone work from American composer/guitarist David First for twelve players. It’s based on the 16th through 32nd harmonics of the note G—a sound world, which resides largely outside of traditional Western musical instruments and training.

Here from Mode Records is a CD release of the work. The disc comes presented in a dark brown and orange coloured mini gatefold featuring a kaleidoscope shape on its front cover. Inside, along with the CD, we have a six-page enlay featuring a write-up about the work and how it was created.

The piece was commissioned by Anthony B. Creamer and premiered at Christ Church (Philadelphia), presented by Bowerbird on February 9th, 2020. The players here, under the banner of The Western Enisphere, take in the following: Jeanann Dara—viola Sam Kulik—trombone, Jeff Tobias—bass clarinet, Alex Waterman—cello, Ian Douglas-Moore—guitar, Tania Caroline Chen—overtone keyboard, Will Stanton—piano, bowed piano, EBow piano, Danny Tunick—tuned glasses, James Ilgenfritz—upright bass, Bern Gann—electric bass, Matt Evans—drum kit, and David First—jaw harp, electric jaw harp, mpe keyboard, all programming.

The piece runs for a total of six nine minutes and forty three seconds. It’s presented as one long track, with five track markers.

To begin with, after a fairly rapid fade-in, the piece focuses down on a very pressing and sustained feel, which seems to hum and very slowly oscillate around your listening space. There is a piercing yet blunt quality to the drone, which suggests the tone of road drills set into notation. As it progresses, you start to notice the presence of different horns, jew harp twang, guitar purr, string crate, and organ simmer. The feel of the piece/ drone largely remains very thick & pressing. And really, the use of the colour brown in the packaging feels very fitting- as if I was to give the piece a colour, it would be thick, heavy & muddy brown- though that’s not to say the different instruments don’t get their place/identity, as the whole thing is well mastered/recorded.

Genre-wise, I’d say Revolutions sits between modern classical minimalism, non-harmonic drone, with forays into thick avant jazz & folk. But there’s no doubt First has his own take on drone form.

items.body: Born in science-fiction novels and developed in philosophy and theoretical physics departments, the " Bootstrap Paradox " is a thought experiment about time travel. It's most easily explained in Back To The Future . Marty McFly, having travelled back in time from 1985 to 1955, finds himself shredding on electric guitar onstage at a school dance, a few months before anyone has ever heard of rock music. Offstage, a man yells into a phone: "Chuck! It's your cousin, Marvin Berry! You know that new sound you're lookin' for? Well, listen to this!" Chuck Berry, of course, is the Missouri singer and guitar player widely credited with inventing rock & roll. So, to summarise. In this alternative history, Chuck Berry hears rock & roll from a kid who heard about it from him . The core idea is this: were time travel possible, it would generate loop-points in time, scrambling the relationship between the past and the future. It's a deeply Spekki Webu move to choose this as an album title. The Dutch DJ and producer, who once described his music as "an intergalactic language that connects people and energies together," has always woven some element of sci-fi mysticism into his music. He's not alone. This is a time-honoured tradition we can trace from Sun Ra to the Electrifying Mojo to Underground Resistance and beyond. In fact, the first track here even shares a title with a Drexciya classic, "Wave Jumper." That said, these retro vibes do not extend to the music itself. Webu's own "Wave Jumper" is a strikingly modern and original piece of music that you can just barely call techno. With a yo-yo-ing, halftime beat at something closer to gabber tempo, and a general aura that's more skate video than warehouse rave. The rest of the album is equally adventurous, and it very much feels like club music's farther vanguard. Less than half the music on Bootstrap Paradox has the kind of galloping 4/4 chug you expect to hear in a nightclub (and to be fair, one of them clocks in at a soaring 153 BPM, beyond the reach of a turntable pitch shifter from most techno records). The rest floats on artfully off-kilter grooves that unfold like origami. Classic genre tropes are thin on the ground. Even the drums are abstract, with none of the sonic links to the physical realm that exist in most club music (no rim shots, no hi-hats, no snares, etc.). The sound design, meanwhile, summons a place both radically futuristic and deeply surreal, a cyberpunk vista through which strange bodies hover, at once abstract and weirdly physical, as if shaped from matter at some confusing middle point between solid, liquid and gas. Radical and mind-bendingly out-there, if not quite avant-garde, Bootstrap Paradox skips any pretense of being arty or experimental in favour of a vibe much closer to the heart of rave culture: trippy, alien and just plain fuckin' badass. In its most conventional moments, Bootstrap Paradox serves up dreamily transportive techno mantras. It's an effect best embodied by "Floating In Acheron," a nine-minute tribal tear-out named after one of the five rivers of the Underworld in Greek mythology. "Moments," the mellowest track here, has the dark soul of illbient artists like DJ Spooky, burying its outline of a beat deep in its ambient murk. The best bits come when we wade further out in the nether-regions, the in-between spaces of rhythm and tempo that few artists explore and that Spekki Webu knows so well. "Axis Point" is an elegantly off-kilter, slow-mo stepper whose groove takes two bars to fully unfold. The album reaches its climax on the final track, "Goodbye Universe," a broken-beat-ish thing that sounds in places like it was played live, off the grid—namely the backwards drum fills that slip just far enough out of time to be both jarring and funky. While the Hague artist might be a lifelong raver, Spekki Webu is still a relatively new artist: he only started DJing in the 2010s and releasing music in the last few years. That might be surprising if you know his records or his DJ sets, both of which have the technique and daring style of a seasoned pro. His music has come thick and fast since his first EP in 2023, and Neural Network , his first album, came out last May. That he's back barely a year later with an even stronger record shows the extraordinary depth of talent at play. On Bootstrap Paradox we hear an artist operating on his own weird frequency, vaulting to the farthest limits of techno and finding incredible things there.

items.body: Bluegrass singer-songwriter Aidan Muse has released “ Progress ,” a new original song inspired by concerns over deforestation and the loss of farmland in his home state of Wisconsin. According to Muse, the track emerged after he witnessed forests cleared and land transferred away from local farmers at what he described as an alarming pace. The song examines the tension between economic development and environmental preservation, with lyrics that challenge the idea of progress when it comes at the expense of natural landscapes and agricultural communities. Throughout the song, Muse questions the long-term impact of large-scale development projects, arguing that promises of future growth often overlook present-day environmental consequences. “Progress” was entirely written, composed, arranged, and produced by Muse. Dave Dalton handled engineering, mixing, and mastering duties. The recording features contributions from Jon Muse on bass, Paul Breitenbach on guitar, Ernest Brusubardis IV on fiddle, Caleb Peters on mandolin, and Aidan Muse on lead vocals and banjo. Buy Progress . Author: World Music Central News Room World music news from the editors at World Music Central

items.body: Angelique Kidjo – Hope!! (Parlophone/Warner Music, 2026) Angélique Kidjo’s Hope!! , her joyful 16-track Afropop set spiced with neosoul, Afrobeats and other popular music influences features a wide range of collaborators, including Pharrell Williams, Quavo, Ayra Starr, Davido, Nile Rodgers, Charlie Wilson, IZA, and PJ Morton. Pharrell produced three songs. Their collaboration began after Pharrell invited Kidjo to perform at his Grace For The World concert in St. Peter’s Square in Vatican City in September 2025. That meeting led to three original songs written and produced in Pharrell’s Paris studio with Kidjo’s voice and style in mind. Among them, “For Me” features Charlie Wilson and focuses on self-celebration in the face of adversity. “No Stopping Us” grew out of a conversation between Kidjo and Pharrell about social change. Meanwhile, “Bando,” which also features Quavo and vocals from Pharrell, draws on the slang term for an abandoned house and points to the street origins of popular trends. Elsewhere, the album is dedicated to Kidjo’s late mother, Yvonne. According to Kidjo, her mother’s favorite song was the moving “Malaika,” which closes the album in an orchestral version arranged by Derrick Hodge and featuring French singer Florent Pagny. Recorded in Paris and Los Angeles over the past three years, Hope!! also includes contributions from The Cavemen on “I’m On Fire,” Fally Ipupa on “Nadi Balance,” Sheila Maurice-Grey of Kokoroko, Dadju on “Superwoman,” and Diamond Platnumz on “Kakua.” In addition, Brazilian artist IZA appears on the “Oyaya.” The album also features “Sunlight To My Soul,” written by Diane Warren, as well as performances by the Soweto Gospel Choir, who previously worked with Kidjo at a 2003 Nelson Mandela benefit concert. Kidjo said the project reflects a message of hope and human connection at a time of growing division. In that spirit, the album continues a career that has paired music with activism, including her work through the Batonga Foundation and as a UNICEF goodwill ambassador. Kidjo’s previous album was her 2021 Grammy-winning album Mother Nature . Buy Hope!! Author: Madison Quinn

items.body:
As the man at the controls at our label showcase at Public Records in 2024, our relationship working together had just started, and his new album ‘Immersion’ (released last month) was in mastering stages. After hearing his opening set, an isolatedmix was written in the stars. 

I technically heard Griff DJ at Brooklyn’s The Lot radio station just a few hours before our label showcase - sharing the booth with him as a temporary groupie while I plastered ASIP stickers all over the walls - and had been deep in his guest mixes prior to us even meeting in person. His journey as a DJ regularly takes him to festivals worldwide, and as part of his connection with Delayed , some intimate sets in the Pocono’s have come to fruition and are a worthy bookmark if you end up liking this one. 

As someone who can traverse a multitude of styles, from ambient and downtempo to deeper house and techno, Griff’s one of those artists that shows up in different ways - every time. Likely because, his music, and the stories around his reasons for his music, are often very personal. Whether it’s a concept, or a vibe, I get the feeling Griff is a master of sense and construct - a pretty special skill for an artist and DJ to have, where stories told come from the heart and have a pure reason. Not performance for performance sake, but a narrative traveling from the mind, told through a meticulous track selection. 

The concept was my attempt to portray various stages of consciousness throughout the morning, from dark into light / sleep to awake, as I get up & start the day & eventually get outside, into the woods for a morning - deep sleep into REM, vivid dreams, waking up from a dream & it's still dark outside but there's a faint glow of light, immersed in nature feeling the warmth of the sun in your face. It starts out cold, dark, alien, otherworldly then shifts towards something more mysterious & inviting but still a bit strange, then moves into warm & fuzzy. Analogous to frost on the ground slowly being melted, warmed & evaporated by the sun. - Aspetuck

items.body: In this edited extract of a conversation recorded at London's ICA on 25 March 2026 for the launch of Shock Factory: The Visual Culture Of Industrial Music, writer and art historian Nicolas Ballet talks to Cabaret Voltaire's Stephen Mallinder about sound, image and subversion Nicolas Ballet: In 1983, RE/Search Publications released the Industrial Culture Handbook, documenting the movement through a cultural project. This handbook, thanks to the introduction by music critic Jon Savage, clearly illustrated all the specific characteristics of the scene, and especially their shock tactics, conceived as a way to subvert the societies of control of that era. This publication included an interview with you and Richard Kirk, ten years after you founded Cabaret Voltaire in Sheffield with Richard and Chris Watson. We can also consult numerous references you provided at the end of the interview: recommendations of records, books, and films. Could you tell us about the context in which Cabaret Voltaire was created? How V Vale and Andrea Juno approached you to participate in this work, which will remain iconic in the field of industrial music? Stephen Mallinder: I should probably answer the second question first, because explaining how we started could easily become a lecture in itself. We began experimenting in 1973, but we didn’t think of ourselves as a band at that point. It wasn’t even just the three of us – there were probably half a dozen people involved. It felt more like a collective. And it wasn’t only about music: we were also interested in film, and everyone had different passions – some were into martial arts, others into cars. We were just teenagers, really, between 16 and 18, growing up in an industrial northern city. We were part of that environment, but at the same time we wanted to transcend it. We were drawn to other worlds – those we saw on television, in films, and heard on records. Over time, things gradually distilled down to three of us – Richard, Chris and myself – focusing on music. But it all started with a loose group of about ten people. There were various comings and goings: for instance, a guy called Mick was in the band for a while, but had to leave when his mother asked for the organ back he’d been playing. We were quite rebellious, but we had a strong interest in art and music, and we felt somewhat separate from many of the kids we went to school with. Eventually, it naturally coalesced into the three of us. Early on, we were particularly inspired by Roxy Music and especially Brian Eno during his time with the band. What fascinated us was the idea that someone could stand on stage with a tape recorder and a synthesizer – what we later learned was a EMS VCS3 – and create these strange, otherworldly sounds. To us, it was just a mysterious machine full of pins and patch cables. All three of us were drawn to that, and I think, in a way, we all wanted to be Brian Eno. That was really the origin. We then spent about three years simply experimenting. To jump ahead a bit: you mentioned ten years, but we had already spent quite some time with V Vale before that. We met him around 1979 or 1980, when we travelled to San Francisco to play a series of shows. At the time, we were signed to Rough Trade, which had launched an American label on the West Coast rather than in New York, believing it would be easier to establish something there. After releasing two albums, we moved over to the West Coast. We arrived in North Beach and were told, “You’re staying in this house.” The door opened, and there was Vale. He was – and still is – one of the most unique and brilliant people I’ve ever met. It turned out to be an extraordinary situation. Not only were we living in his house, right in the middle of North Beach, but he also ran City Lights Bookstore. Through him, we suddenly had a direct connection to William S Burroughs and the entire Beat movement. We found ourselves immersed in this strange, esoteric, and incredibly stimulating cultural world. The reason we later worked with Vale is simple: we lived with him. We shared that space with him, Andrea Juno, and Mark Pauline. At the time, Vale was just beginning what would become his Research series, but he was already publishing an extraordinary newspaper – not really a fanzine, but a large-format broadsheet – called Search & Destroy, which he co-edited with Andrea. We stayed close after that. We would return and spend time with him over the years. In fact, much later, if you look at the cover of The Covenant, The Sword And The Arm Of The Lord (1985), it features the three of us alongside Vale and Andrea. What connected us was the way he bridged art, literature, music, and attitude – he was deeply connected, and through him we became part of that wider cultural network, including the Industrial Culture Handbook. Vale later came to Sheffield and stayed with us for a while. He was an extraordinary character – one of the most beautiful people you could meet. I remember taking him on the train from London up to Sheffield. As the train passed through Leicester, he looked out of the window and exclaimed, “Oh my God – Leicester!” He was completely fascinated. For him, northern industrial England was exotic. He loved the canals, the rough pubs – everything about it. And he’s still out there, still active, still doing remarkable things. That’s how our relationship with him began, and why it lasted. NB: Yes, he’s still selling his own books, in front of City Lights in San Francisco! SM: Exactly, and the funny thing is, when we first knew him around 1979-1980, nobody knew Vale’s age. And we still don’t know, but he’s still going, so I think he’s immortal. I hope he is. NB: I hope too! Talking about Vale, he was very into, and still is today, the theories of William S Burroughs, such as you were, in a way, with Cabaret Voltaire and the cut-up technique, but through noise. And this is very interesting because it was a time when you defied order and control through noise. In the foreword you wrote for Alexander Reed’s book, Assimilate: A Critical History Of Industrial Music (2013), you said: “Although most at the time were unaware of many of the readings into the inherent political and social power of noise, it was clearly a language of subversion. Noise defied order and control. It was a musical taboo. Sonic belligerence. It could destabilise. This was not entertainment, but it was fun.” Regarding the fun part, could you tell us more about the first gig by Cabaret Voltaire in 1975? Because I understood it was a bit intense, especially for you. SM: Yes, I got thrown off stage and ended up in hospital. It’s become a bit of a legendary story. What’s funny is that, when you look back on it, there’s a certain strange logic to how it all unfolded. The whole thing ended in a riot – unsurprisingly, in retrospect. What we didn’t realise at the time was that we were playing in front of a crowd of engineering students whose main interests were rugby and beer. They weren’t exactly predisposed to experimental electronic music. And yet, that was our very first proper gig. In truth, the situation was something of a misunderstanding from the outset. We had spent a long time working in a loft, experimenting, staging odd happenings, even playing music to people randomly in the street – what you might call a kind of sonic terrorism. Eventually, we thought we should try performing in a more formal setting and see what would happen. The opportunity came through Chris. Someone he knew had a friend involved in an environmental group – something called Science For The People, I think – and they were organising a benefit concert. They asked Chris if his band would play. He said yes. When they asked what kind of music we made, he more or less told them whatever they wanted to hear: disco, pop, soul – everything. So we arrived having been billed as something entirely different. Instead, we came on stage playing tape loops and generating this dense, abrasive noise. There was also a visual element: projected film loops – probably Standard 8, before we even moved on to Super 8 – and Richard wearing a jacket covered in Christmas lights, plugged directly into the mains, which meant he could barely move. He was literally tethered to the electricity supply. I can’t remember us performing anything resembling a conventional song. We were just producing noise – intentionally so. Our idea of performance was rooted in chaos. We wanted to provoke a reaction, to create disruption. That, for us, was the point. And we certainly got a reaction. The audience stormed the stage, attacked us, and a fight broke out. Some friends helped pull us out of it, but it quickly escalated into a small riot. In the end, I was thrown off stage and ended up in hospital. It makes for a good story, but beneath it lies something more fundamental about our approach. From the beginning, our aesthetic was about shock, disturbance, and confrontation. That was our understanding of art at the time. Even the name Cabaret Voltaire was chosen for its provocation. The reference to Cabaret Voltaire – the birthplace of dada – carried an idea of disruption and anti-conformity that resonated with us. That was exactly what we were trying to do. NB: Yes, regarding the dada influence, you said that it “offered a guidebook of how to go about deconstructing a world that did not adequately represent the one we actually inhabited”. You also crossed paths with the members of Throbbing Gristle, who also released some Cabaret Voltaire recordings from the 1970s on Industrial Records. You shared with them a rejection of the British government of the time and the social and political difficulties it created. This system no longer allowed for belief in the hippie utopias of the 1960s. This critical perspective can be found in the album Red Mecca (1981), in which you criticised British participation in the war in Afghanistan by revealing “the dark heart of Thatcher’s Britain”, according to Martin Lilleker. The fact that the group was named after the Cabaret Voltaire says a lot about your approach. Did this link to art history serve to re-enchant reality, through a new relationship with art, a new way of thinking? SM: At that point in time, we were really trying to find fluid ways of expressing what we were doing. At the same time, we were very aware that, as individuals, we are inherently complex – and inherently political. We never wanted to separate our work from that dimension. Not in terms of party politics, but in the sense of recognising the inequalities and tensions that structure the world, and finding ways to point to them. Sound was one of our primary tools for doing that, but it wasn’t the only one – we also worked with visuals. What mattered to us was exploring different forms of expression, and how they could intersect. Red Mecca came out of that approach. It’s really about the power of words – the effect produced by placing two terms side by side. At the time we were working on it, we had also started making videos, and this coincided, quite strikingly in hindsight, with the Iranian Revolution. That context fed directly into our work. We incorporated imagery of Islamic fundamentalism, not in a purely critical or dismissive way, but as material to be juxtaposed. For instance, we would place images of Ronald Reagan alongside those of religious extremists. The word ‘red’ carries a whole range of associations – socialism, blood, violence – while ‘Mecca’ evokes a specific place, but also a broader idea of the East and of spiritual centrality. What interested us was precisely the tension between those meanings. We wanted to bring them together, almost collide them, without prescribing a fixed interpretation. It wasn’t about promoting a particular ideology. Rather, we were trying to provoke questions – to confront people with the contradictions of the world they inhabit. In a way, our work was about presenting those contradictions as they are, and saying: this is what surrounds you, this is what you’re living through. That was the impulse behind Red Mecca, and more broadly, what we were trying to do at the time. NB: The most conflicting aspects of the post-industrial system lead you to explore the theme of mind control, which is found in particular in the album The Voice Of America (1980). The titles “The Set-Up”, “Control Addict”, “Silent Command”, “War Of Nerves” or even “Spread The Virus” signal the group’s interest in the sort of mental conditioning you saw emanating from the US in the 1970s and 1980s. In the book Tape Delay (1987) by Charles Neal, you said: “We live and breathe like an American culture in England. It’s just throwing it back in another context.” These titles are also a clear reference to the idea that 'the word is a virus’ by William S Burroughs and his The Electronic Revolution. How did you approach the theme of mind control in the world of Cabaret Voltaire? SM: Yes, that was the world we were living in. It was just before Margaret Thatcher came to power, though her rise was already underway. At the same time, there was a strong awareness of American influence – what we would have understood then as a form of imperialism. What strikes me now is how relevant many of the themes we were engaging with still are, and also how their meaning has shifted. Take, for instance, The Voice Of America. At the time, we were interested in it as an example of media operating as a tool of influence, even indoctrination. Yet today, in a different context, it can be perceived as a voice of liberty. That kind of reversal is quite telling. More broadly, we were very attuned to the mechanisms of media. In the late 1970s and early 1980s, not everyone was thinking in those terms – but within certain circles, including groups like Throbbing Gristle, there was a growing awareness of how information and entertainment were becoming increasingly intertwined, and how propaganda functioned within that overlap. These are ideas that have become much more widely understood today, particularly with the rise of social media. But at the time, we were already thinking about questions of control – social control, the shaping of perception, the structures of power. Our references often came from literature, from writers like Franz Kafka, whose work explores precisely those kinds of systems. In a sense, what we were doing was simply reflecting those concerns back into the world – making them visible, or at least more perceptible. Looking back, it feels as though many of those concerns have only intensified, which perhaps explains why the work still resonates today. NB: What is fascinating about historical industrial groups is seeing how these artists anticipated very early on issues surrounding the media that are still relevant today. And we can also find different military elements in the artworks of Cabaret Voltaire, which could be compared to Industrial News, edited by Throbbing Gristle. Do you feel like you were taking part in the information war of industrial music at that time? SM: I don’t think we ever saw ourselves as partisan. The risk, when you take that position, is that you end up reproducing the very problem you’re trying to criticise. It’s a difficult balance – a kind of tightrope. We tended to think of ourselves more as observers, almost like journalists: taking what was in front of us and reassembling it, collaging it in a way that might allow people to see it differently. That was really the intention. The goal was simply to make people think – not to make them think like us. Everyone is free to draw their own conclusions. It was never our role to tell people what to think. That’s a trap you can easily fall into: believing you hold the truth, that you can somehow ‘liberate’ others by imposing a particular viewpoint. We wanted to avoid that entirely. The moment you start doing that, you risk becoming a form of propaganda yourself – part of the very problem rather than an alternative to it. What interested us instead was creating a shift in perception – presenting things differently, so that people might question them for themselves. NB: It could be violent and grotesque too at the same time. SM: I think another important aspect was our engagement with taboo. At the time, we approached it quite naively – we were younger, and it was very much of that moment. We deliberately played with subjects like militarism or overt political imagery because we felt that confronting those taboos could disrupt perception. The idea was to produce a kind of shock – something that might jolt people into a different awareness. With hindsight, I think we’re more cautious about that approach, and rightly so. We now have a better understanding of how people can be affected by these things, and how easily certain strategies can turn against their original intention. Part of the issue is that what begins as provocation can quickly be absorbed and neutralised. You only have to look at punk rock: something that started as a radical, disruptive force was rapidly co-opted, becoming commercialised and widely consumed. Once that happens, the original charge is lost. The same risk applies to working with taboo. Elements that were once confrontational can become aestheticised, turned into consumable objects. And at that point, their critical force is largely diminished. So I think it’s important to remain attentive to that dynamic. At least for me, there’s now a greater awareness of how these processes operate, and a corresponding need for caution. NB: Video was also a very important medium in Cabaret Voltaire. For example, you and Richard can be seen posing with a Portapack Sonore on the cover of The Crackdown. Video was so important that you started Doublevision in 1982 to release video works by Cabaret Voltaire and other industrial/experimental artists. The release of Doublevision Presents: Cabaret Voltaire allowed you to add moving images to your sound compositions, with the help of filmmaker St. John Walker for some videos. How did you approach this medium, at a time when music videos are increasingly commercialised worldwide? SM: I think it comes from the fact that we never really saw ourselves as musicians so much as artists. That gave us the freedom to move between different media quite naturally. In fact, even before the concert we mentioned earlier – the one that ended in a riot – we had already staged what you might call our first performance. It took place at the Edinburgh Festival fringe, probably the summer before. The only problem was that we couldn’t afford the train fare to get there, so we didn’t attend in person. Instead, we created what we called a ‘concert package’. We sent it to the festival, and it was presented in our absence. It consisted of a reel-to-reel tape, a Super 8 film, and a series of printed handouts – cut-ups and montages. In other words, it contained all the elements of a performance, just without the performers. The audience experienced it as a kind of distributed concert. We later learned that Lol Coxhill was present and even played along with the material as it was being shown, which is quite extraordinary. But we weren’t there – the film was screened, the tape was played, and the audience engaged with the printed material. That approach says a lot about how we thought from the beginning. We were always interested in multimedia, in combining different forms. As technology evolved – particularly in electronic music and film – it became more accessible and easier to use, which allowed us to push that integration further. We started with Super 8, but as soon as new tools became available – video, then later digital cameras – we adopted them immediately. It wasn’t about being purist or attached to a specific format; we were interested in what each medium could offer. Super 8, for instance, could be transferred to video, which made it much more malleable as a material. Our influences were already pointing us in that direction. Beyond Roxy Music, we were deeply inspired by The Velvet Underground, as well as by Andy Warhol and his Exploding Plastic Inevitable (1966-1967). The idea that images could create a kind of hypnotic texture – just like music – was very important to us. So, visuals were always part of what we did. By the 1980s, the available technology simply made it easier to integrate them more fully into our work, and we embraced that without hesitation. We were never interested in limiting ourselves to one medium – we wanted to use everything that was available. NB: Your video practice aligned with the spirit of the industrial genre, both in its multidisciplinary nature and in the topics you addressed through this medium; in Doublevision Presents, you used footage of New Guinean tribes and Shiite rituals, but also images from pop culture and other various sources (medical procedures, military parades and riot footage), captured either from the television news or from the archives. How did you come up with the idea of ​​working with these different archives? SM: I’m not sure I can give a single, definitive explanation. As you were describing it, what struck me is how much of it relates to ritual. That’s something we’ve always been drawn to – those forms of behaviour through which people try to make sense of the world. We’ve consistently been interested in what you might call the esoteric, or practices that exist on the margins. For instance, much later, when we made “Don’t Argue” (1987) in America with Peter Care, we included documentation of an actual voodoo ceremony. That kind of material fascinated us – not in a purely anthropological sense, but as a way of engaging with systems of belief and representation. At the same time, there was a strong interest in working with found footage: bringing together contemporary images, television broadcasts, archival material, old films. That impulse was always there. But beyond that, it was really about process. Our method was based on montage and juxtaposition – placing things side by side and seeing what emerged from that encounter. Often, the results were unexpected. We would discover connections or tensions we hadn’t anticipated. In our live performances, for example, the visuals and the music were constantly shifting, and the way they aligned was never fixed. Each iteration produced a different set of relationships. What mattered to us was precisely that moment of collision. We weren’t aiming for coherence in a conventional sense. The work wasn’t meant to make sense in a linear or unified way. Instead, it was about creating points of friction – instances where images and sounds collide, fragment, and recombine into something new. In that respect, the material itself often came from places others might overlook or avoid. We were drawn to what lay at the margins – discarded images, overlooked footage, fragments found on the periphery. Those were the elements we wanted to bring into play. That, ultimately, is what guided our approach. NB: This may also be a way of showing the paradoxes of Western societies between violent images and more consensual images in popular cinema and popular culture in general. SM: Yes, absolutely. We still live in an intensely violent society, and there’s always a risk of turning away from that reality. What has changed, perhaps, is the way that violence is mediated. Today, we exist in what Guy Debord described as the ‘society of the spectacle’, where everything becomes image, performance, and representation. In that context, the distinction between what is real and what is constructed becomes increasingly difficult to grasp. When we were working, there was a stronger sense – at least from our perspective – that what we were engaging with remained more directly connected to lived reality. Now, I think many people struggle to locate a reality that feels stable or coherent. There’s a sense of living within a kind of simulation, where experience is constantly mediated and reframed. In a way, it feels as though we were anticipating some of these developments, even if we didn’t fully articulate them at the time. What we were doing was rooted in that specific moment, but looking back, it also seems to resonate strongly with the present – particularly in terms of how we understand media, perception, and reality itself. This is something I’ve been thinking about again recently, especially with the renewed activity around Cabaret Voltaire. It brings into focus the extent to which earlier work now reads almost as a form of prefiguration. At the time, though, much of it was intuitive. We didn’t necessarily have a fully formed theoretical framework for what we were doing – we were artists, and we were working instinctively. It’s really only in retrospect that some of those ideas begin to take on a clearer shape and meaning. NB: You also composed the soundtrack for Peter Care’s film Johnny YesNo (1982). I guess the working method was very different here: did you adapt to the film, or did Peter Care direct his shots according to your universe? SM: We didn’t really know how to approach it at the time – we had to invent our own method as we went along. No one was telling us how to compose a film score. We worked directly with the rushes that Peter Care brought into the studio. He would come down, we’d project the footage onto the wall, and we would simply play along to it. In that sense, it was almost like performing a live soundtrack. That’s how the ideas emerged: by responding in real time to the images. There wasn’t much room for editing or rearranging. We couldn’t manipulate the material in the way you can today. Instead, we focused on capturing the atmosphere of each scene – finding the right mood and playing to it as it unfolded. It was very immediate, very instinctive. I imagine the process is quite different now. Contemporary composers often construct soundtracks with a high degree of precision, using digital tools to map sound to image. At the time, though, it was much more direct – we were essentially making it up as we went along. But it worked for us, and it was a lot of fun. In many ways, scoring Johnny YesNo felt like playing a live concert. We approached it with the same energy and responsiveness. We also had an ongoing relationship with Peter Care, which made the collaboration very natural. Around the same period, we worked on other projects in a similar way. For instance, we contributed to Salvation! (1988), and New Order were also involved in film scoring at the time. The approach remained largely the same: we received the rushes and responded directly to them. There were no digital timelines, no screens to synchronise everything in advance. You created the soundtrack first and then found ways to align it with the images afterwards. It was a very hands-on process. The same applies to Chance Versus Causality (1979), made with Babette Mondini. That piece was recorded in the studio in a single live take. Nicolas Ballet would like to thank the ICA team, especially Hannah Geddes, Eray Yilmaz, Tom Heardman, Steven Cairns, Ken Eno and Beni Asante, as well as Stephen Mallinder's manager, Steve Malins. Shock Factory: The Visual Culture Of Industrial Music is published by Intellect. The Wire 499 featured a ten page special of essays and interviews exploring the visual and sonic world of Cabaret Voltaire. Buy a copy of the issue here. items.body: The soundtrack to a new film about the Denver heavy metal four-piece takes the listener deep into an exploration of outer – and inner – space Photo credit: Alessandro di Martino In 2024, Blood Incantation released Absolute Elsewhere. One of the strangest, most compelling and original albums in heavy music of the past decade, it connected with a wide variety of listeners – many within and, crucially, an equal number outside the metal underground.The album used cathartic, whirling death metal with cerebral, unexpected pastures (ambient music, analogue synth freakout, gloriously complex prog passages, vintage kosmische panache) and – as is always the case with Blood Incantation – some serious world building. As intimate with Popul Vuh and Tangerine Dream as Morbid Angel or Death, Absolute... items.body: Is it possible to protect a family member from the horrors of war? This question was posed in the film “Life Is Beautiful,” which inspired Ukrainian artist Halyna Andrusenko to create her own works of art, which in turn inspired the documentary by Joel Espi and the score by Daniela Mars, and whose title is shared by the opening track. Since the early days of the invasion, Ukrainians have been wrapping monuments and statues in cloth and reinforcing them with sandbags to protect them from fire and bombs. In her art, Andrusenko does the same with her family (allowing them to breathe of course) and draws sketches of them: a brand of performance art translated to physical form. Through flute and wordless voice, Mars conveys feelings of love and protection, with a melancholy undercurrent that highlights the fragility of human life. “Life Is Beautiful” is short yet sweet, a choral preface to the overture. Mars’ multitracked voice becomes that of a church choir, blurring the lines between baptism and requiem. Threaded into the following piece, the voice becomes the accompaniment for an array of flutes, operating as an additional instrument. Even without seeing the film, one can imagine the tenderness shown by Andrusenko as she wraps her family fold by fold, and the mixed feelings as she ties the cloth in string. “Colours of the Bending River” operates in the lower register, a cluster of dark thoughts. “Dana Nobis Pacem” (“Give Us Peace”) cements the spiritual connection. Part of the Latin Mass, the phrase also appears in works by Beethoven and Vaughn Williams. This prayer leads to the first of three versions of “Halyna’s Theme,” which is also the first of two contrabass pieces that represent the album’s emotional center. The contrabass take on “Dark Sky Lullaby” conjures images of its title; in Ukraine, these skies are as often caused by war as by weather. “In the Sky” is the score’s most abstract piece, a shimmer of dismay including a disturbing rustle at 00:50. Light and dark continue to battle, Mars’ voice a perennial reminder of hope. The later tracks grow more intimate with the sound of breath. “Halyna’s Theme (by the water)” offers early confidence, communicated by multiple flutes, before one steps to the fore, is heard and is then joined again, a parable of community. “Dark Sky” is balanced by “Silent Light,” the title a sideways allusion to “Silent Night.” We don’t know how the film ends, because we don’t know how or if the invasion ends. We do know that the war will leave a residue of sorrow. Mars conveys this beautifully in “The Wind Breathes,” leaving us with the bittersweet feeling of a mother who does what she can, knowing that it can never be enough. (Richard Allen) If you are in Kyiv, be sure to check out the exhibition, which just opened at the Dymchuk Gallery run by Max aka Trinidad Shevron!

items.body: Empusae and Maris Anguis have crafted a fantastic album that rewards repeated listening and offers a welcome step toward a more spiritual and cultural focus for their label Cryo Chamber. A cinematic, immersive dark ambient soundscape approach Onryōtan by Empusae & Maris Anguis   Addictively creepy and unsettling, Onryōtan provides a lovely and terrifying musical introduction to the rich supernatural lore of Japan, from monstrous yokai to vengeful onryo spirits to black curses by scorned women and much more. Belgian musician Empusae (Nicolas Van Meirhaeghe) brings a cinematic, immersive dark ambient soundscape approach, while Tokyo-born and Illinois-based Maris Anguis (Ryo Utasato) contributes a more organic approach with traditional Japanese instruments alongside synths and a haunting, mournful, enchanting voice. The album consists of seven tracks—two solo compositions from each artist, and three collaborative ones. Each track ranges from five and a half to seven and a half minutes, which is long enough to be immersive, but short enough to provide a nice diversity of approaches. The opening collaborative track, “Eien no Yami” (“Eternal Darkness”), sets the stage by building a haunted soundworld that threatens to swallow the listener whole. For me Ryo Utasato’s voice steals the show—I think sung vocals are underused in dark ambient, especially female ones, and here one can easily imagine them coming from the mouth of a vengeful female spirit. Listening feels like floating in a thick fog that clings clammily to your clothes as the gates to the land of the dead creak open with an otherworldly scream. “Kurozuka” follows with a reimagining of the famous Japanese man-eating ogress Kuromitsu, who haunted the black mounds for which the track is named, devouring unwary travelers who accepted the invitation to sleep in her cave. This is one of Maris Anguis’ solo compositions, and I appreciated the mix of electronic ambience, percussion, and traditional Japanese stringed instruments, which together build a hushed, haunted feel punctuated with moments of pure screaming terror. The very stones seem to whisper both an invitation and a warning. Next up is “Tename” (Tenome), named after a yokai monster that has eyes in the palms of their hands rather than on their face. This is one of Empusae’s solo tracks, and falls more on the black ambient side. The listener gets a sense of a vast darkness surrounding them everywhere they turn, through which curling mist-tendrils drift, clutching at you with clammy fingers. The track ends in silence, as if evoking the moment after the monster has sucked out the victim’s bones. A driving, twisted ritual atmosphere :: “Ushi no Koku [Mairi]” is another collaborative track, and one of my favorites on the album. The name refers to a “shrine visit at the hour of the ox,” the blackest part of night between 1 and 3am, when the boundaries between the worlds of the living and the dead are at their thinnest. This is when a scorned woman can visit a shrine unseen for seven nights, pounding nails into the temple’s wood that cause wracking pain to their victims, and/or summon an evil spirit to devour them. Ryo Utasato composed an entire album with Fabio Keiner on this subject a few years ago, so it’s not a surprise that this track is a standout. Drums build in the background throughout the track, overlain with immersive dark synths, which together create a driving, twisted ritual atmosphere. Ryo Utasato’s vocals powerfully evoke the feelings of the wronged woman performing the ritual, while a chorus of the damned joins in horrific sympathy. Maris Anguis’ solo track “Mukaebi” comes as something of a relief, evoking the fires that the faithful light during the festival of Obon to guide the spirits of the beloved dead back to their homes for a new year visit. The track opens with a gong as the gate to the land of the dead creaks open. Eerie flutes trace the journey of the dead souls to home and back. The chanted chorus intoning as wood blocks are struck gives the track a deeply spiritual feel. The last shared track, “Chimatsuri,” tells the story of a blood rite in which an enemy soldier is sacrificed as a blood offering to ensure success in a battle. Synths slowly build an oppressive feel as inky black fingers of night reach out to touch and then ensnare the victim. Deep drums drive the horrific ritual forward, thudding like blows falling upon an already shattered body spouting blood as a hellish offering. Flutes add a sense of nervous tension and a longing for release from this dark spell. Empusae closes out the album with “Teke Teke,” whose name refers to the click-clack sound that the vengeful spirit of a young woman is said to make as it scuttles faster than a speeding car after its victims with its hands and elbows alone, since its legs were sheared off by a passing train. The synths craft a thick, suffocating miasma that surrounds the listener. Tension slowly builds throughout the track: is that a skittering sound in the distance? Low drums sound ominously, flutes twitter like unseen spirits, and a mournful female voice moans her sorrow and rage. My only quibble is that I wish the digital version of the album listed the instruments played on each track—I got the sense that traditional Japanese instruments were being used, but I would love to know which ones. Translations of the lyrics that Ryo Utasato sings in Japanese on two tracks would also be cool. In any case Empusae and Maris Anguis have crafted a fantastic album that rewards repeated listening and offers a welcome step toward a more spiritual and cultural focus for their label Cryo Chamber. Onryōtan is available on Cryo Chamber. [Bandcamp] Onryōtan by Empusae & Maris Anguis

items.body: Originally published in Melody Maker on May 11, 1996, Mark Roland’s review of Meat Beat Manifesto’s Subliminal Sandwich captured the arrival of a record that would go on to become one of electronic music’s most influential and genre-defining releases; republished here with permission, 30 years on. A feast of beats and all manner of exotic electronica Forget all those “Now That’s What I Trip Hop” compilations. Forget also all the half-arsed post-modern samplist outfits who regurgitate large chunks of old soundtrack albums, couch it in cod theatrical mystique and are thought of as weird by people who play the album at dinner parties. Meat Beat Manifesto are back. Jack Dangers has spent the last several years plunging into what could have been a one-way expedition into the history of sound. Before he made the step from post-rave dance progenitor, author of blueprints taken up with gusto by the likes of The Prodigy, The Future Sound Of London and Transglobal Underground, to pith-helmeted explorer lost in the jungle forever, Jack Dangers has managed to deliver this massive missive. Spread across two CDs (for a limited time, anyhow), Subliminal Sandwich is a feast of beats and all manner of exotic electronica. A one-way expedition into the history of sound :: On first listening there’s an apparent schism between the two CDs. The first is recognisable as your standard format; songs, some singing here and there, all in all not a radical departure from 1993’s Satyricon. Cut-ups from old toasting records have produced two of its most thrilling tracks; “Nuclear Bomb,” an irresistible rhythmic assault of dub bass, lush textures and the ranting toaster, and “Assassinator.” The monstrous “Cancer” a melancholy and bleak excursion, is another spine-shuddering high point. The second CD is a non-linear monster of an achievement. Apparently, the whole thing was put together using some super synth from the Seventies, the sort of gear used to generate sonic blurts for analysis on an oscilloscope. It’s not one long gasbag of sub-Orb pointless noodling though the machine has been coaxed into jumping through all manner of hoops. “Mad Bomber/The Woods” provides an eminently suitable future soundtrack from the inevitable TV movie about The Unabomber while, as the rest of the CD gathers pace, gradually building into an almost painterly swipe of colours and textures. It arrives at Ketamine-induced nirvana with “Stereophrenic and “Simulacra” and understated, barely contained frenzy with “Electric People” This record won’t be scorching into the Top 10, but all your favourite household names will be first in the queue to buy it. You really should be joining them. items.body: Gabriele Poso has been releasing music since 2008, through Yoruba Records, BBE, Soundway, Wonderwheel and Mr. Bongo. For his sixth album he started his own imprint, AG Records, and recorded Maraviglia live to tape with a full band in an analogue studio in southern Italy. “Contigo Mi Vida” is the second single from the album, out on 19 June. Emanuele Coluccia leads on horns, moving between saxophone, flute and trumpet over Afro-Cuban percussion and a groove rooted in late-’70s Italian disco and Afrobeat. Poso’s vocals run effected and dubbed-out through it. Maraviglia also features Andrea Rossetti on piano, Fender Rhodes, Hammond and Moog, Davide Codazzo on bass, Antonio De Donno on drums and percussion and Alberto Zacà on guitar. Listen to “Contigo Mi Vida” HERE and pre-order Maraviglia via THIS LINK The post Daily. Discovery: Gabriele Poso – Contigo Mi Vida appeared first on Rhythm Passport.

items.body: Review by Fercandio46 — Excesses...in arrangements, in length, nothing was enough for the successor to Don Giovanni, and Le Tr'sor de Valliesres, Versailles' third album, boasts the colors of many macarons mimicking a rainbow. Guillaume de la Piliere sings and plays guitar as if it were the most furious rock, but with Alain de Lille on piano and keyboards, creating that palatial symphonic atmosphere...which, being French, always has a guillotine lurking about...half threat, half hope, depending on your perspective. The cabaret piano perfectly complements the streetwise edge, giving freshness to the complex arrangements and making them immediate, coexisting with Renaissance-like sections where the band becomes precise and brings together the land of Charles Aznavour and Johnny Hallyday with Rush and Genesis.Exquise Betise continues to create grandiose atmospheres like Genesis, but with a prominence in the execution of the drums, bass, and keyboards that leaves no time to trace influences... instead, it immerses you in the offered proposition, full of subtleties and pure symphonic rock with a French touch. Une Saint Barthelemy Devote has that folkloric tenor present in Foxtrot, along with the musicality of Michel Berger, and bass lines by Olivier de Gency without which it wouldn't be the same. Alain de Lille's keyboards are reminiscent of the early, raw Tony Banks of Nursery Cryme.And the next section becomes both rock and psychedelic, with synthesizers and a chorus in which everyone participates. They speed up...and stop speeding up...only to do it again, discovering new sounds in the process. In the middle there are parts that recall Pink Floyd's Echoes, but then their virtuoso execution takes them to other territories, the guitar here with a David Gilmour sound at the service of the infidelities in carved walls, secret passageways, and organs that hide surprises like Magma-style choirs, while a jazzy piano improvises...breaking schemes, challenging the monarchy with the sharpest anarchy.In Viendra L'heure the electric guitar together with the keyboard carve an ornate canvas on which they will sing, with Guillaume as soloist, reaching the enveloping psychedelia of The Doors, until a wind unites the theme to the next, the flamenco Jadis, where the spirit of Steve Hackett floats alongside Manuel de Falla.Degenerescence Obsessionnelle takes over with counterpoints of bass and guitar...bathed by the keyboard like the sea bathes the beach, and yes...Hackett is heard again, along with a harpsichord, until a keyboard section like a choir with bass and mellotron that recalls Yes, recreates the atmosphere of Heart of the Sunrise, only until Guillaume sings and the melody, half longing for the past, half promise of the future, continues on. At times Olivier de Gency sounds like Chris Squire without sounding like an imitation, and there are moments where they take flight and sound like themselves, a product of the place that saw them born and gave them their imprint; there we see the Galeries Lafayette, as well as the Banlieues de La Goutte d'Or.That street-style Hammond organ rock from the beginning returns in Avec Tous Mes Hommages, full of harmony in the keyboard and guitar notes...playing classic hard rock solos, until the whole band sounds like the best Yes in blue, blanc et rouge.Le Tresor des Valliesres ends as the album began, with an explosion of colors suggested by the keyboard and guitar notes, a cathedral under whose wide roof whispers burrow, as well as stretched notes...until dissonant guitar and bass notes, as if King Crimson were forcibly taking the farewell, and the atonality throws off balance...paradoxically, to increase the level reached, it confirms with each note that freedom, which makes us live in equality, and only in this way will fraternity arrive.

items.body: Review by siLLy puPPy — My gawsh, there are three bands named DERIVA in Spain! One was a Basque rock band formed in 2001from Donostia-San Sebasti�n, another post-metal band from Madrid that released one album in 2016 andthen finally the subject of this review, an all-instrumental mostly solo project of guitarist /bassist / drum programmer Javier Hern�ndez from Soria in Castilla y Le�n. Hernandez played invarious bands including Sol Negro and Pangea before finally setting some of his pent up ideas freeon this project with guitarist Carlos Rubio along for the ride. Rubio played in some of the samebands in the future. This DERIVA project has so far only released a single album titled ECLEPSYSwhich came out in 2012 and showcases these two seasoned musicians cranking out 16 tracks ofinstrumental prog metal.Pretty much an album out of the Joe Satriani type of guitar savvy hard rock and progressive metalinstrumental playbook, this album finds the two guitarists delivering melodic riffs and solos alongwith only a bass and programmed drums but despite the lack of players involved here actually comesoff pretty dynamically delivered with a series of strong tracks that navigate various techniques,exotic mood settings and rhythmic formats. A few touches of keyboards offer the occasionalatmospheric presence but for the most part this is a brawling dudes only jamfest where two guitarsduke it out while keeping their eyes on the melodic prize. The duo play together seamlessly and mostsurprisingly the drums actually sound fairly real. The production is also top notch which adds tothe squeaky clean feel of the album.The opening "Estrella del este" sets a strong tone with a mystique of the Middle East findingthrashing stomping power chords with ethnic flavors reminding me a bit of the Australian band BaKonly sans the vocal charm. "Life Groove" jumps into more progressive territory while "Babel" offersa bit of alt metal flavor. A few ballads enter the scene with tracks like "Es Por Ti" offeringslower clean guitar sounds mixed with crunchy leads which in this case reminds me of some of thoseho hum Pikes from Buckethead that never seem to end. While the duo never runs out of steam as far astheir playing abilities are concerned, the album does suffer from too much of a good thing withoutany true break from the same formula strewn out in different melodic motifs. More stylistic shiftsand tone changes would've gone a long way towards making this lengthy release less monotonous by thetime the end nears. "Moonster" is a nice change with echoey twangy guitar tones and escapes themetal vibe altogether.Overall this is one of those fairly competent examples of a musicians stockpile of ideas coming tofruition in one chock-filled display of opportunities finally realized. All in all it's acaptivating album that delivers on all fronts and for what it is, it's really a great album howeverthere isn't really anything new under the sun as albums like this were being cranked out as far backas the 1980s so there has been no shortage of similar minded guitarists releasing such examples eversince. These two dudes do a great job with the limited resources they are presenting and given thatit's basically two guitars, a bass and drum program it's well done however it's not one of thosealbums that will make you feel like breaking the bank to run out and get. For one thing i keepwishing the two would break into more daring metal diversity but that never really happens. By thetime the album ends it sounds like a retread of everything that came before which is more likelythan not given no vocalist on board to distract from what sounds more like background music to lyricoriented songs. Good but not great.

items.body: Review by andrea — "Sunlight" is the second album by Drift Lab, a jazz rock project based in Rome and led by Manuele Montesanti. It was self-released in 2026 with a completely renewed line-up featuring, along with founder member, composer and leader Manuele Montesanti (piano, synths), the new members Marco Pistone (bass), Guido Della Gatta (guitars) and Roberto Porta (drums) plus the guest Carlo Maria Micheli (sax). According to the official website, this is music "written with rigour but performed with freedom, where improvisation finds its home within intricate harmonic architectures". Drift Lab is an open, constantly evolving project, aiming to shape a sound that blends "jazz roots and contemporary imagery, instrumental virtuosity and electronic curiosity, composition and experimentation". The art cover tries to give a visual form to the musical content...Electronic sounds and a brief drum roll introduce the album's title track, "Sunlight". It's a bright piece, full of frenetic energy, ready to wake us up to face a new busy day. A kind of urban ride illuminated by the sunlight...The following "Yellow Fire" is a piece with a jagged rhythm but full of warmth and melodic flares that leads to "Bump" a jazz rock track full of nocturnal and disquieting atmospheres with excellent interweaving of guitar and keyboard that share the solo parts, supported by a never banal rhythm section..."A-M-M-I-M" somehow revisits and reinterprets a piece from the previous album ("M-I-M-M-A"). It's a relaxed track that at times invites you to dance the night away while "Serendip" is a slow, sensual piece featuring guest saxophonist Carlo Maria Micheli and a certain oriental exoticism. The title refers to the ancient name of the island of Ceylon..."Chaste Countrywoman" starts with the bass in the foreground that traces a funky rhythm, then the electric guitar outlines melodic paths that take the song in other directions... Next comes "Bleep" is a complex and fast piece where all the musicians showcase great technical skills and a notable interaction."bYpOLAR" begins with an old video-game atmosphere and continues with irrepressible freshness, alternating more relaxed moments with others where the pace becomes pressing and lively. Ten, the dreamy "Evolving" concludes the album. A beautiful official video was shot for this piece, completing the sonic universe the band has evoked with images of a disturbingly beautiful dystopian future...On the whole, an excellent fusion work!

items.body: Review by alainPP — Franck Carducci, playing music based on the progressive foundations of Pink Floyd and Genesis, moved to Amsterdam to play and survive. Theatrical prog rock, heavy rock reminiscent of Genesis and Led Zeppelin."Sheeple," with its bleating and swirling organ, evokes Pink Floyd and Deep Purple, forcing us to revisit the genre. "Self-Righteousness" boasts a raw, 70s sound, reminiscent of Whitesnake's old-school, fruity hard rock, with the dripping organ of this band playing good old-school, uncensored music. Barth unleashes a heavy, bulldozing solo. "Sweet Cassandra," the first of three tracks, features a narrative French-Anglican voice, while the harmonica, reminiscent of Supertramp, provides a soothing ballad. A nostalgic, sentimental tune that resonates. "The Betrayal of Blue," already heard on the 2023 live album. A Beatles-esque crescendo with an explosive verse, C�dric's oozing organ, Lea's furious pads, and Barth daring to play a solo reminiscent of bygone days?this young upstart is very good, navigating between two unique musical facets. The alternation of early heavy prog, with Mary's melting theremin break before the martial reprise, pads worthy of Genesis and Deep Purple. The exhilarating final crescendo flirts with the Wallian era, modern and old overlapping with the little dancer in her bottle?a touch of nostalgia. "Sweet Cassandra," a reprise with its Gabriel-esque flute, its marshmallow melody, a charismatic bucolic atmosphere."The Limits of Freedom," a chilling Genesis-like intro, a popular hard rock variation. A fresh, melodic interplay, a no-nonsense nod to a time before prog metal existed. Franck's other, more powerful rock side plays out its two distinct styles with his mischievous sidekick, featuring a frenetic guitar solo and a frenetic piano finale reminiscent of certain American bands. "Love or Survive" has a Supertramp-esque flavor, with its charming melody, piano, and subtly woven female backing vocals. It builds to a gradual crescendo, culminating in a seemingly endless bluesy guitar solo that evokes the emotion of yesteryear. The basic break, with its raw vocals and piano, transforms into an old-fashioned melody. The thunderous organ kicks in, providing a Beatles-esque chorus to conclude this crescendo, a musical comedy of guitar and organ intertwined. "Sweet Cassandra" returns to the bar scene named after Cassandra, ending with a syrupy vocal, creating suspense before launching into "Do What You're Told," bringing the band back to its acoustic melody worthy of Oldfield. Franck is hardly inventing anything new in revisiting our classics. A prominent bass, a southern feel, piano bar rock to free us from societal constraints and finally do what we want before the end of time.
